findings.title: ConsistencyFM drops the consistencyfm_hyperparameters arg; loss always runs hardcoded boundary=1
findings.claim: `ConsistencyFM.__init__` accepts `consistencyfm_hyperparameters=` (sde_lib.py:9) and both training paths pass `config.consistencyfm.to_dict()` into it (run_lib.py:96, run_lib_pytorch.py:100), but the body never reads that argument — it unconditionally hardcodes the dict above. The loss reads it at losses.py:150/167/234/237 via keys `delta`/`num_segments`/`boundary`/`alpha`, so every run uses boundary=1 regardless of the config. Separately, the configs declare key `delta_t` (not `delta`), so even if the argument were honoured the loss's `hyperparameter["delta"]` (losses.py:167) would KeyError. Verified by AST in _audit_code/out/hyperparameters.json: param present, never used in body; hardcoded boundary==1; README schedules boundary 0 then 0.9.
findings.concern: The README's documented CIFAR-10 and high-res training recipe explicitly runs a two-phase boundary schedule (`--config.consistencyfm.boundary 0` then `0.9`, README:47-49,78-80); because the argument is discarded, both phases train with boundary=1, so the reproduction recipe for the headline FID cannot be followed as written (the boundary curriculum is a silent no-op).
findings.resolution: Assign `self.consistencyfm_hyperparameters = consistencyfm_hyperparameters` (falling back to the default only when None), and rename the config field `delta_t`→`delta` (or read `delta_t` in losses.py); then confirm which boundary schedule produced the reported numbers.

findings.title: Broken isinstance guard: `if (threshold, int) and threshold == 0` (tuple always truthy)
findings.claim: This guard (also at losses.py:220) is meant to be `isinstance(threshold, int) and threshold == 0` — the correct idiom is used at losses.py:203. As written, `(threshold, int)` builds a non-empty tuple that is always truthy, so the guard collapses to `threshold == 0`.
findings.concern: The intended int-vs-float distinction (per the code's own comment at sde_lib.py:37) is lost; it is currently inert only because boundary is hardcoded to int 1 (see hyperparameters-ignored) and the used values agree, but a float `0.0` boundary would silently take the wrong branch (demonstrated in _audit_code/out/threshold_tuple_bug.txt).
findings.resolution: Replace with `isinstance(threshold, int) and threshold == 0` at losses.py:184 and 220.

findings.title: README CIFAR eval reads ckpt 34-40 but the documented training saves only ckpt 0-10
findings.claim: Checkpoints are named `checkpoint_{step // snapshot_freq}.pth` (run_lib.py:150, run_lib_pytorch.py:160). The CIFAR config sets `snapshot_freq = 20000` (cifar10_gaussian_ddpmpp.py:34) and the README trains to `n_iters 200001`, so from-scratch training produces checkpoint_0 … checkpoint_10, but the documented eval command requests indices 34-40.
findings.concern: A user reproducing Table 2 from scratch and running the documented eval command hits the `while not exists: time.sleep(60)` wait loop (run_lib.py:272-276) forever, because checkpoint_34.pth is never produced; the eval indices presumably match the separately provided Google-Drive checkpoints, but this is undocumented.
findings.resolution: Authors: state the snapshot_freq used for the released checkpoints, or align the README eval indices with the training snapshot_freq.

findings.title: High-res Dataset.__getitem__ ignores idx and reseeds global numpy RNG every call
findings.quote:
def __getitem__(self, idx):
    np.random.seed()
    idx = np.random.randint(0, self.num_imgs)
    img_name = os.path.join(self.root_dir, '%d.jpg'%(idx))
findings.claim: For CelebA-HQ / AFHQ-Cat, `__getitem__` discards the DataLoader-supplied `idx`, calls `np.random.seed()` (entropy reseed) on every access, and returns a uniformly random image (with replacement); the AFHQ variant (lines 52-61) does the same inside a bare `try/except: continue`.
findings.concern: Despite `config.seed = 42`, the training data stream is nondeterministic and reseeds the global numpy RNG on every item across all 8 workers, so a high-res run cannot be reproduced bit-for-bit; impact on the reported FID (measured over 50k samples) is negligible, but exact-run reproduction is impossible.
findings.resolution: Index by the provided `idx` and seed numpy once per worker via `worker_init_fn`; remove the per-item `np.random.seed()`.

findings.title: Headline '4.4x / 1.7x faster' convergence claim has no code to compute it
findings.quote: significantly improves training efficiency by converging 4.4x faster than consistency models and 1.7x faster than rectified flow models
findings.claim: The repo trains only Consistency-FM and evaluates its FID; there is no baseline (Consistency Model, Rectified Flow) training code, no logged baseline FID-vs-step curves, and no script that computes a convergence-speed ratio. The one figure that this number comes from (Fig. 1) needs all three curves.
findings.concern: The abstract/Fig. 1/§4.1 headline efficiency ratios cannot be reproduced or checked from this repository; they depend on baseline runs that are neither included nor pointed to (baseline FID numbers in Table 2/3 are likewise cited, not recomputed here).
findings.resolution: Provide the baseline training/curve artefacts (or references to the exact runs) and the script that reads off the 4.4×/1.7× crossover, so the efficiency claim is reproducible.

findings.title: Loss target uses stop-grad online model (θ⁻=θ), not the EMA network as Eq. (6)/(8) state
findings.quote:
with torch.no_grad():
  if (isinstance(hyperparameter["boundary"], int) 
      and hyperparameter["boundary"] == 0): # when hyperparameter["boundary"] == 0, vr is not needed
    vr = None
  else:
    vr = model_fn(xr, r*999)
    vr = torch.nan_to_num(vr)
findings.claim: The target-branch velocity `vr` (and hence `fr`) is computed with `model_fn = model` (losses.py:196), i.e. the current online network under `torch.no_grad()` (stop-gradient), not the EMA weights. The EMA (`state['ema']`) is maintained but applied only at sampling/eval (run_lib_pytorch.py:165-168, losses.py:293-297).
findings.concern: Eq. (6) and Eq. (8) define the target with θ⁻ = 'the running average of past values of θ using EMA', whereas the code uses θ⁻ = θ (stop-grad); the two are different training objectives, though the code's variant is valid and is exactly the θ⁻=θ case that Theorem 1 analyses, so impact is limited.
findings.resolution: Either use the EMA parameters for the `vr`/`fr` target to match Eq. (6)/(8), or state in the paper that the released model trains with a stop-gradient (θ⁻=θ) target.
